content.text: Trigger finger is caused by friction and inflammation of the FDS with development of an inflammatory nodule near the distal palmar crease.

items: Most commonly affects the A1 pulley (at MCP joint)
When the finger is flexed, the nodule slides proximally under the pulley
When the finger is extended, the nodule must slide back distally — this can be difficult
Can affect any finger, including the thumb
Palpable / audible click or clunk
Pain develops
Cannot actively extend finger — must use PROM to extend
May not be able to extend finger even passively (most severe)
Insidious onset of finger clicking and occasional locking
Recent history may include activity requiring increased grip frequency or force
Relative rest improves the condition, but clicking/locking returns once activity is reintroduced
Small palpable nodule may be felt around the MCP joint
Tenderness at rest and pain during extension
Is this a new activity, or recent change or sudden increase in activity?
AROM shows reduced extension with a click, lock, or clunk (may be observed and/or heard)
PROM is similar to AROM, with potential difficulty extending the finger
RROM shows reduced finger extension strength from disuse
Muscle weakness may occur in finger extensors from disuse
The muscle belly of FDS is likely to be normal length, despite the tendon gliding problems
Dupuytren's: normally painless, consistent stiffness of the fingers, with dimpling of the palm
Trigger finger: normally painful with a clear clunky, clicking, or locking motion during extension

content.text: Management is based on reducing inflammation and friction.

items: Modify or remove offending activities
Splints or orthoses (many varieties available)
Corticosteroid injection may be given
If unsuccessful, surgery may be elected — addresses the A1 pulley (not the tendon or nodule)

content.text: Post-surgery: Because scar tissue follows surgery to the A1 pulley, PROM is used immediately after. Once AROM is full and pain-free, strengthening exercises are given.

items: Promote muscle balance in forearm and hand
Improve joint function (normal joint play)
Treat compensatory structures to restore overall function
Promote joint nutrition with mid-range pain-free PROM of the hand and wrist
Restore normal joint play with joint mobilisations to wrist and carpals
Restore normal muscle balance with NMT & MFR to forearm
Decrease trigger point activity in muscles around hand and forearm

content.title: Cautions
content.text: Do not work on site or provide heat to the affected nodule (respect acute stage of healing precautions). Be careful with finger flexion and extension; avoid deep flexion of the finger.

The vast majority of cases resolve without the need for surgery. Resolution can be difficult — it is important to avoid aggravating the tendon or increasing inflammation or friction. Timelines are variable.

quiz.question: Which structure is most commonly affected in trigger finger?
options: The A1 pulley at the MCP joint
quiz.explanation: Trigger finger most commonly affects the A1 pulley — a piece of connective tissue that keeps the tendons of FDS in place as they cross the MCP joints.

quiz.question: If surgery is performed for trigger finger, what structure is surgically addressed?
quiz.explanation: Surgery addresses the A1 pulley (not the tendon or nodule). Because scar tissue follows surgery, PROM is used immediately after.

quiz.question: Heat should be applied directly to the affected nodule in trigger finger to reduce inflammation.
quiz.explanation: Do not work on site or provide heat to the affected nodule — acute stage of healing precautions should be respected.
